options: Rational choice limited by information, brain power and time
Refusing to buy anything over a set price
questions.why: People try to choose well but are limited in what they know, what they can process and the time they have.

questions.q: Which is the best example of bounded self-control?
options: Comparing three phone contracts and picking one
Knowing you should stop eating crisps, but finishing the bag anyway
questions.why: You know what is best but lack the willpower to do it.

questions.q: Match each bias to its meaning.
pairs: Relying too much on the first number seen
Judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind
Doing what others around you do
questions.why: These are the four biases named in the specification.

questions.q: A restaurant puts a £90 steak at the top of its menu so that a £35 steak seems reasonable. Which bias is it using?
questions.why: The first high number sets a reference point that makes later prices feel low.

questions.q: After a burglary in the street, residents think burglaries are far more common than the data shows. Which bias is this?
questions.why: A recent, vivid example comes to mind easily, so it seems more likely than it is.

questions.q: Giving blood for no reward is difficult to explain if people only ever act in their own self-interest.
questions.why: Altruism, caring about others at a cost to yourself, challenges the assumption of pure self-interest.

questions.q: In an experiment, Person A splits £10 with Person B. If B rejects the offer, both get nothing. B rejects an offer of £1. What does this suggest?
options: B cares about fairness as well as money
questions.why: A purely self-interested person would accept £1 over nothing. Rejecting it shows that fairness matters.

questions.q: Explain one way in which behavioural economics challenges the traditional assumption that consumers are rational.

ideas.label: Traditional theory assumes people weigh costs and benefits to maximise utility
But real people are limited or biased, e.g. bounded rationality, bounded self-control, anchoring

questions.model: Traditional theory assumes consumers are rational and maximise their utility. Behavioural economics shows that people have bounded rationality and use biased shortcuts such as anchoring, so their choices can differ from what the rational model predicts.
questions.why: Set out the assumption, then the real behaviour that breaks it.

tests.answer: Traditional theory says people maximise utility, but they have bounded self-control so they overspend.
People use rules of thumb when they shop.
Prices go up when demand goes up.
